the fast path —
no container,
runs every commit

span.p:
8 Postgres stores
+ an engine to dispose

div.style: color: rgb(11, 37, 69) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
the services
each writes through to its own store

div.style: color: rgb(74, 56, 0) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
memory is NOT 'no persistence'. It builds real stores, so the
write-through path runs on the DEFAULT configuration and in every
test — rather than only when somebody remembers to start a
container. That is exactly the shape that produced B7: code that
was correct and never ran.

div.style: color: rgb(90, 45, 0) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
the divergence this caught within an hour. SQLite ignores
foreign keys unless asked, so an orphan row was refused by Postgres
and accepted by SQLite — the same test passing on one backend and
failing on the other. A fast path that enforces LESS than production
is worse than no fast path. PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON, now with a test.

div.style: color: rgb(90, 45, 0) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
the suite has its own DATABASE (D79). It builds tables with
create_all and drops them on teardown — which against the dev
database deletes everything AND leaves alembic_version stamped at
head with nothing behind it. Then 'upgrade head' is a silent no-op
and the app dies at startup. Separation makes it impossible.
